title: Methotrexate Side Effects: Nausea, Folic Acid and When to Get Help
meta_title: Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Help and Warning Signs
meta_description: Managing methotrexate nausea, mouth ulcers or fatigue? Read practical steps, folic acid evidence, medicine checks and when to seek urgent help.
excerpt: Practical help for weekly methotrexate side effects, with clear urgent warning signs and an honest look at what folic acid can and cannot prevent.
direct_answer: Mild nausea or tiredness may be manageable, but new cough, breathlessness, fever, bruising or bleeding needs urgent medical advice. Take methotrexate once weekly for arthritis and folic acid as prescribed. Severe breathing difficulty or a serious allergic reaction needs 999. Never wait for symptoms after an overdose.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: methotrexate side effects, methotrexate nausea, folic acid, mouth ulcers, methotrexate fatigue, weekly methotrexate safety
content:
Quick answer: Methotrexate can cause nausea, a sore mouth, tiredness and other side effects. Simple food and fluid changes may help mild symptoms, but persistent or new symptoms need a medicines review. Take prescribed folic acid exactly as directed. For inflammatory arthritis, methotrexate is taken once a week, not daily. Seek urgent advice for fever, unexplained bruising, new breathlessness or a troublesome cough. Severe breathing difficulty or signs of a serious allergic reaction need 999.

First check: mild symptoms and urgent warning signs

This guide is for adults taking low-dose weekly methotrexate for inflammatory arthritis, not cancer treatment. It helps you prepare a conversation with your pharmacist, rheumatology nurse or prescriber. It cannot tell whether a symptom is caused by methotrexate, your arthritis, an infection or another condition.

  • Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, such as gasping or being unable to get words out, or a tight or heavy chest. Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, struggling to swallow, collapse or rapidly worsening breathing can be a serious allergic reaction. Do not drive yourself to A&E.
  • Tell your doctor or seek urgent advice immediately for a new troublesome or persistent cough, new breathlessness, fever or shivering, a sore throat with feeling unwell, yellow skin or eyes, unexplained bruising or bleeding, or a marked change in how much you pee. NHS guidance advises contacting your doctor or 111 immediately for these possible serious effects. In Northern Ireland use your GP out-of-hours service if your practice is closed. Use 999 for an emergency.
  • If you have taken more methotrexate than prescribed, or taken it daily instead of weekly, get urgent medical advice now. Do not wait for symptoms. NHS guidance directs people to 111; in Northern Ireland contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service immediately if you appear well. If advice is not quickly available, go straight to an emergency department. If seriously unwell, call 999 or go to an emergency department, as nidirect poisoning guidance advises. Take the packet and your medicine list if asked to attend hospital.

Do not wait until the next routine blood test or try to treat warning signs with extra folic acid. Ask the clinician what to do about your next methotrexate dose. Follow any individual illness plan your rheumatology team has already given you. This is different from changing or permanently stopping treatment yourself because of a mild symptom.

Make the weekly routine unambiguous

For rheumatoid arthritis and similar inflammatory conditions, take methotrexate only once a week on the agreed day. It is not an extra painkiller for a bad joint day. Keep it separate from daily medicines, check the label and keep your patient card available. Never take two doses together to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what you took or when, ask a pharmacist or your prescribing team rather than guessing.

Methotrexate treats inflammation and helps protect joints; it does not provide instant pain relief. Feeling better is not a reason to stop it without a review. Equally, a suspected serious reaction or infection needs timely clinical advice, not a blanket instruction to continue regardless. See the NHS weekly-dose and overdose guidance.

Nausea, appetite and diarrhoea: practical first steps

For mild nausea, try simple meals and avoid rich or spicy food. Smaller meals may be easier than a large plate. If you vomit, small, frequent sips can help reduce dehydration. Peeing less or having dark, strong-smelling pee can be a warning that you are becoming dehydrated. If you have a prescribed fluid restriction, ask your team how to manage fluids safely.

Do not automatically repeat a methotrexate dose after vomiting; ask your pharmacist or prescriber what to do. Check before adding an anti-sickness or diarrhoea medicine. Persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, trouble keeping fluids down or feeling increasingly unwell needs prompt medical advice, not a two-week home experiment.

If nausea recurs around your weekly dose, keep a short note of its timing, duration, eating and drinking, folic acid use and any other new medicines. Ask whether your prescribed folic acid plan needs review, whether an anti-sickness medicine would help, or whether changing from tablets to an injection is suitable. NRAS describes these options; an injection may reduce nausea for some people, but it is not a guarantee or a change to make yourself.

Folic acid helps, but it is not a cure for every side effect

Folic acid is usually prescribed alongside methotrexate to reduce some unwanted effects. Follow your own prescription for its dose and days. It is generally taken on a different day from methotrexate. If the label or clinic instructions are unclear, ask before changing anything. A shop-bought multivitamin is not a substitute for prescribed folic acid, and extra supplements may duplicate it.

A Cochrane review published in 2013 included six trials with 624 adults with rheumatoid arthritis. Folic or folinic acid reduced gastrointestinal symptoms, abnormal liver blood tests and withdrawal from methotrexate. Evidence for preventing mouth ulcers was less certain: the apparent reduction was not statistically significant. There was not enough information to draw reliable conclusions about blood-cell complications. The review did not show a significant loss of arthritis-treatment benefit.

This is older evidence, not a promise about your individual symptoms or proof that supplementation prevents all toxicity. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service notes limited evidence for the best folic acid schedule and describes several clinician-led regimens. Do not copy a different schedule from someone online.

A sore mouth, fatigue or hair thinning deserves a specific conversation

Mouth ulcers: contact your pharmacist or rheumatology team for advice, especially if ulcers are new, recurrent or affect eating and drinking. Mention the exact weekly methotrexate routine, folic acid and every other medicine. Mouth ulcers can be a sign of toxicity, particularly alongside a sore throat, fever, bruising or bleeding. Those combinations need urgent assessment rather than just a mouthwash.

Tiredness or drowsiness: do not drive, cycle or use machinery while affected. Pace necessary tasks and record whether tiredness follows the weekly dose or is present all week. If it persists, ask for a review. Arthritis activity, infection and other conditions can also cause fatigue; do not assume every change is an unavoidable medicine effect.

Hair thinning: NHS guidance says this is unlikely to be permanent. Tell your prescriber if it bothers you. They can review treatment options. Do not reduce methotrexate yourself or buy high-dose supplements without checking interactions.

Blood tests and medicine checks still matter when you feel well

Keep every arranged monitoring appointment. Blood tests check your blood count, liver and kidneys; some problems are picked up before you feel a symptom. Testing is usually more frequent when treatment starts or changes, with the exact schedule set by your team. Normal previous results do not mean a new fever or breathing symptom can wait.

Before any new prescription, pharmacy remedy or supplement, say that you take weekly methotrexate and show your patient card. The SPS interaction guidance warns about trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole because of severe bone-marrow suppression risk. If either is proposed or supplied, alert the prescriber or pharmacist promptly so they can check it. Do not choose your own alternative antibiotic.

Do not buy oral ibuprofen, naproxen or painkiller-dose aspirin without checking first. Some people are deliberately prescribed an NSAID alongside methotrexate with specialist advice and monitoring; do not stop an existing prescription simply because an interaction is listed. This article is not a complete interaction check. Herbal products and supplements are not automatically safe.

Alcohol, sun and pregnancy questions

Ask your team about alcohol based on your methotrexate dose, liver tests and other risks. NHS guidance says alcohol is usually acceptable with low weekly doses for inflammatory conditions, while Arthritis UK notes some rheumatologists advise stricter limits. That is not a personal safe allowance or a reason to start drinking. Read our alcohol and arthritis guide; your prescribing team's advice comes first.

Methotrexate can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. NHS advice is to avoid bright sun, wear protective clothes and use SPF 30 or higher; do not use sunbeds or sun lamps.

If you become pregnant or think you may be pregnant while taking methotrexate, contact your specialist promptly. Ask before trying for a baby or changing contraception. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea can affect contraceptive-pill protection, so follow the pill leaflet and ask a pharmacist if unsure. This guide does not set pregnancy washout periods or replace specialist advice.

Take this short list to your next review

  1. My weekly methotrexate day, prescribed amount, formulation and folic acid days are: ____.
  2. The symptom starts ____ after the dose, lasts ____, and affects eating, drinking, sleep or work in these ways: ____.
  3. My other prescriptions, pharmacy medicines and supplements are: ____.
  4. Do I need a treatment change, extra monitoring or symptom treatment?
  5. Who should I contact urgently, and what is my plan for the next dose if I develop an infection or serious symptom?

For more about monitoring in later life, see our methotrexate safety guide for older adults. This page focuses on recognising and discussing side effects, not adjusting doses. key_takeaways: For inflammatory arthritis, methotrexate is taken once a week, not daily. Get urgent advice after any overdose; do not wait for symptoms.
Folic acid can reduce some side effects, but does not replace blood tests or prevent every serious reaction. Follow your prescription.
New cough, breathlessness, fever or unexplained bruising needs urgent advice. Severe breathing difficulty or a serious allergic reaction needs 999.
